sections.title: Who else is doing this, and how do they validate?
sections.intro: Public information only, searched on 2026-11-12. Marketing pages rarely give methods, so many cells say 'none public'. We make no claims about any company's private data or methods.

items.s: Site: 'next-generation biodefense'; frontier AI systems that identify biological threats and design medical countermeasures in real time.

p: None stated on the public site. Investors listed include OpenAI Startup Fund, Lux and Founders Fund; $30M announced Oct 2025. UNVERIFIED: any data claim.
None public. A press piece quotes a response-time claim ('months to hours') and notes it is the company's own and has no independent testing cited.

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: Cannot be compared with anyone until it publishes a benchmark or a customer test. For a buyer, the question is which of the validation types below it has done.

items.t: SecureBio (and the Nucleic Acid Observatory work)

p: Expert-written Virology Capabilities Test: 322 multimodal questions.
Public benchmark. Experts averaged 22.1% in their own sub-areas; o3 scored 43.8% (arXiv). Wastewater sensitivity is a statistical model on public-health data for 16 viruses (retrospective, preprint).

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: A knowledge test of models, not a test of a detector. Good for what it is.

items.t: DNA synthesis screening: SecureDNA, IBBIS, Aclid

p: Curated sequence-of-concern databases.

NIST built a blinded 200 bp benchmark and gave SecureDNA, IBBIS and MITRE sets of 1,000 sequences (200 true positive, 200 true negative, 600 ungraded). We did not find NIST's results. IBBIS's false-positive claim (under 2%) is UNVERIFIED. Aclid's site gives ROI numbers with no method.

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: The NIST design is the most independent: the developers did not build the test. Marketing ROI figures tell you nothing about accuracy.

items.t: Ginkgo Biosecurity / Perimeter (airport and wastewater surveillance)
items.s: Close the gap between threat detection and response.

p: Claimed: 8 airports, 135+ countries of origin, 2,600+ wastewater samples since 2021.

Company-reported anecdotes: H3N2 subclade K flagged 7 days before public repositories; vancomycin-resistant Enterococci a week before clinical identification; four test-and-evaluation exercises. No denominators.

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: Interesting data footprint, but 'we saw it first' stories without how many misses and false alarms cannot be scored. Whether Perimeter and Ginkgo Biosecurity are the same entity is inferred from a redirect.
Plants covering about 30% of the US population (independent estimate).
Independent: 254 counties, median correlation with cases 0.904 in 107 counties, but 21.5% of counties below 0.8. Company: 0.96 correlation for influenza A in 2023-24 (not independently verified).

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: The independent analysis is the better model: it reports the weak tail, not only the median.
No proprietary data; open platform.

czid-bench generates simulated reads and scores recall and QC pass rate per organism. A Genome Medicine paper (2025) added resistance detection on four clinical cohorts plus wastewater. No prospective accuracy study found.

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: Closest in spirit to our benchmark: constructed truth plus open code.
2,000 validation samples; 15,000+ patient dataset (company).

Prospective study of 350 sepsis patients (Nat Microbiol 2019): sensitivity about 93% against a composite standard; specificity 62.7% by microbiology alone, or 76.3% after clinician adjudication. A 2023 validation used 2,000 samples. The lead author is a company employee.

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: The best lesson here: the same test goes from 62.7% to 76.3% specificity depending on the reference standard. Always ask what the truth was.
UCSF-derived clinical data (company).

Nature Medicine paper with UCSF; summaries report 21.8% (48 of 220) infections found by sequencing alone in a cohort over 1,000 patients (UNVERIFIED, paper not opened). Analytical validation used remnant CSF plus contrived samples; an RCT of about 400 patients was reportedly launched with no results found.

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: Retrospective plus contrived samples: reasonable first steps; the RCT is the step that would matter.

items.s: Predict antibiotic susceptibility from whole genomes.

p: Genomes with measured susceptibility from 40,000+ isolates.

Tested on 956 clinical isolates from a different site and time (April to August 2023): 96.9% categorical agreement over 7,801 calls; very major and major error 1.4% and 0.8%; ResFinder baseline 83.5%.

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: The closest to the validation design we want: separate site, separate time, a baseline to beat, error types reported.

items.t: Arc Institute (Evo 2) and protein-design companies (Profluent, Basecamp Research)
items.s: Open genomic foundation model; AI-designed proteins; a biodiversity sequence dataset.

p: Evo 2: open OpenGenome2. Eukaryotic viruses were excluded from training. Basecamp: BaseData in 28 to 30+ countries (company claim).

Evo 2: zero-shot variant effects and generation checks; Arc says the viral exclusion weakens prediction for human viruses and red-teaming found outputs 'effectively random' for pathogenic viral proteins. A fine-tuning preprint on 110 human viruses reported AUROC 0.6 for SARS-CoV-2 escape variants. Profluent: wet-lab editing in human cells (company figures). Basecamp: no independent validation found.

kids.t: How much to trust it (our reading)
p: Honest about a limit (viral exclusion), which is rare. Not pathogen-detection evidence.

items.t: What recurs, and what is worth believing
items.s: Seven validation styles, ranked by how much they can tell you.
list: Prospective cohort with an orthogonal reference (Karius, nanopore study): strongest, but the reference standard moves the answer.
Blinded or held-out testing by someone else (NIST benchmark, Genome Research CSF study): strong.
Separate site and separate time (Day Zero isolates): strong for genomic models.
Independent correlation that reports the weak tail (Biobot county analysis): good for surveillance.
Retrospective cohorts with clinician adjudication (Delve, Karius clinical impact): useful, softer.
Benchmarks and red-teaming (SecureBio, Evo 2): measure models, not detectors.
'We saw it first' anecdotes and ROI claims (Perimeter, Aclid): cannot be scored.

items.s: Almost nobody publishes a prospective, geographically separate, time-split test of AI pathogen identification.
p: Day Zero comes closest, for resistance. For open metagenomic classification the public record is simulated data (CAMI, CZ ID) and a handful of PCR-confirmed clinical sets (a 13-dataset viral comparison found only 3 of 13 pipelines caught low-abundance and mixed infections). That is where a small, open, honest benchmark like this one can help.

sections.title: What working with the Department of War means, and what data moves
sections.intro: Facts from public sources, 2026-11-12. We describe the process in general and make no claims about any company's private contracts.

items.s: Department of War is a secondary title; the statutory name is still Department of Defense.
p: A 2025-09-05 executive order authorised 'Department of War' for official correspondence and public communications. Contracts and statutes still say Department of Defense unless Congress acts. We did not check whether a rename has since been enacted.
src: Military.com on what the order does legally

items.t: How a startup typically gets in
items.s: A call or solicitation, a paid prototype, scenario tests, then maybe production.
list: Entry points: JPEO-CBRND 'Work With Us' pages and requests for information, SBIR/STTR, consortium Other Transaction Agreements (for example the Medical CBRN Defense Consortium), and Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) commercial solutions openings.

DIU biosurveillance (2025-03-25): 78 responses; prototypes awarded to Bana Solutions, Booz Allen Hamilton and Cyberhill Partners with data.world and KUNGFU.AI; prototyping 12 to 24 months; next step is simulated scenarios. No metrics or production path published.

DIU ANTIDOTE wastewater (2025-01-22): three milestones, ingest genomic data and return results, report on chemical-biological-defense networks, and pass an independent verification and validation exercise in a remote, disconnected setting. No quantitative metrics published.
A prototype award is not a production contract. We found no production decision for these programs.

items.s: Public, controlled unclassified, or classified; the tier decides where the code can run.

kids.t: Impact levels (vendor sources, check the current guide)
list: IL2: public or non-critical data
IL4: controlled unclassified information (CUI)
IL5: higher-sensitivity CUI and national security systems
IL6: classified up to SECRET
A July 2025 DISA update reportedly folded non-national-security CUI into IL4
GISAID: registration and a Database Access Agreement; no passing data to unregistered third parties; one feed was cut off in Jan 2026 over redistribution.
Select agents (42 CFR Part 73) govern possession, use and transfer of agents and toxins, not sequences.
Export controls: one DIU performer is described as covering threats on the Commerce Control List and Australia Group lists. Whether sequence data itself is export-controlled was UNVERIFIED.
Inputs: wastewater genomic data and diverse data sources, plus manual methods tied to predefined pathogen lists
Outputs: early warnings, biorisk recommendations, analytic results on network reports, visualisations
Schemas, confidence formats and risk-score definitions are not public (UNVERIFIED)

kids.t: Our own version of the shapes
p: In this repo: input is a Kraken2 report, a MetaPhlAn profile or a table of species and percent; output is a report of what the result supports, does not support and what to check next. For a real deployment you would add the sample metadata (collection place, date, host, protocol) as required input and a calibrated confidence plus the evidence trail as output.

items.t: How these tools get evaluated in public descriptions
list: DARPA Bio-ALIRT: detection algorithms tested on real military and civilian data from five cities, with natural outbreaks standing in for releases.
Standard metrics: sensitivity, specificity, timeliness and false-alarm probability.
NIST CAISI and UK AISI public work mostly tests models for dual-use uplift, not detectors. NIST AI 800-3 asks benchmark reports to state statistical assumptions and uncertainty.
Frontier Model Forum: say whether a result is an automated benchmark, a red-team exercise or a controlled trial.
We found no public BARDA, CDC or DHS method for evaluating AI detection tools.

items.t: What this implies for our evaluations
list: Report sensitivity and false alarms with confidence intervals, plus time to detection.
Use realistic and held-out scenarios, including an independent run in a disconnected setting.
Keep the harness runnable offline on public or synthetic data and portable to a controlled enclave.
Make outputs auditable: calibrated confidence, abstention, and a saved evidence trail.
State the design: benchmark, red team or trial. Test contaminants, low abundance and missing metadata.
